42858214.label: Background
42858214.text: Hydatid disease (HD), also known as echinococcosis, is a parasitic disease caused by tapeworms. HD is endemic in many parts of the world and can affect virtually any organ system. Due to the rapid growth of worldwide migration, especially in recent decades, the disease can be diagnosed anywhere, particularly among immigrants in non-endemic areas.

42858214.label: Objective
42858214.text: To illustrate the spectrum of abdominal imaging manifestations of HD and to review the principal benign and malignant abdominal cystic lesions that can mimic HD, using an organ-based approach with emphasis on imaging features that aid in differential diagnosis.

42858214.label: Findings
42858214.text: Radiologic imaging is crucial for diagnosing HD, assessing disease activity, progression, and complications, and detecting stage- and organ-specific features. Hydatid disease in the abdomen can mimic other abdominal diseases, depending on the organ involved. Additionally, many other abdominal lesions can mimic hydatid disease and present with similar clinical symptoms. This pictorial review demonstrates characteristic imaging findings of HD and its mimics across the different abdominal organs and spaces, highlighting specific morphological features and potential diagnostic pitfalls. This review incorporates the World Health Organization Informal Working Group on Echinococcosis (WHO-IWGE) classification to provide a standardized framework for describing the imaging appearances of cystic echinococcosis.

42858214.label: Conclusion
42858214.text: Recognizing the characteristic imaging features of HD and its mimics is essential for accurate diagnosis and appropriate management. A systematic approach that incorporates lesion morphology, organ involvement, disease stage, and relevant clinical and epidemiological information can improve diagnostic confidence, enable early diagnosis, and help avoid misdiagnosis and inappropriate intervention.

42867514.label: Objectives
42867514.text: The introduction of improved multi-agent systemic therapies has made restaging and treatment response assessment in patients with localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) increasingly complex. This scoping review aims to assess and compare methods for local disease restaging and treatment response assessment in localized PDAC, with a focus on their association with resectability, overall survival (OS), and R0-resection rates.

42867514.label: Materials and methods
42867514.text: This scoping review included studies on restaging in patients with PDAC following systemic therapy using CT and PET/CT from MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL.

42867514.label: Results
42867514.text: Among 4680 identified studies, 20 fulfilled the eligibility criteria. Most (n = 15) studies analyzed CT, and 5 analyzed PET/CT. Groups of restaging methods included new response categories, size-based metrics, volume, vascular contact, tumor attenuation, fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT derived metabolic parameters, and resectability criteria. Dual-energy CT-derived extracellular volume (DECT-ECV) was evaluated as a baseline predictive biomarker. Associations between restaging methods and outcomes were reported inconsistently: some studies found significant associations for specific methods, whereas others did not. No restaging method showed a consistent association with both R0-resection and survival across all studies.

42867514.label: Conclusion
42867514.text: Restaging of localized PDAC after systemic treatment remains challenging due to the limited accuracy of RECIST 1.1, particularly for the classifications partial response and stable disease. The current evidence suggests that integrating additional imaging features, alternative imaging modalities, and the biomarker carbohydrate antigen (CA)19-9 may improve the assessment of resectability and prognosis. These findings support a future version of RECIST 1.1 to alert clinicians to this issue.

42867514.label: Key points
42867514.text: Question How effective are current (PET/)CT-based restaging methods in assessing local disease resectability and prognosis in localized PDAC after modern multi-agent systemic therapy? Findings Current restaging methods show inconsistent association with R0-resection and survival; RECIST 1.1 is particularly limited for the assessment of partial response and stable disease. Clinical relevance Current evidence confirms a need to integrate additional imaging features and the biomarker CA19-9, during restaging in patients with localized pancreatic cancer after modern systemic therapy to improve accuracy and reduce the risk of missed treatment options.

42880964.text: [18F]F-AraG is a clinical-stage PET tracer in immuno-oncology that accumulates in activated T cells and tissues with high mitochondrial biogenesis. Characterizing its distribution in individuals without malignancy is essential for interpreting immunometabolic states relevant to cancer biology. Methods: Twenty adults without active malignancy underwent a single [18F]F-AraG PET/CT scan, with tracer uptake assessed in relation to clinical history, medications, and demographic and physiologic factors. Results: Bilateral brown adipose tissue activation was identified in 3 participants receiving potentially brown adipose tissue-activating medications, in the absence of cold exposure or fasting. One showed elevated vertebral bone marrow uptake, previously linked to poor survival in immune checkpoint inhibitor-treated lung cancer. One of 2 participants with breast implants showed asymmetric periimplant uptake. Posterior pulmonary uptake occurred in a subset of participants, often with prior respiratory conditions and thoracic lymph node uptake. Conclusion: Whole-body [18F]F-AraG PET captures diverse immunometabolic activity in individuals without malignancy, reflecting systemic processes that may influence cancer and treatment outcomes.

42886364.text: Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) has become integral to the detection, localization, risk stratification, and management of prostate cancer. Increasing utilization of prostate MRI in screening, active surveillance, targeted biopsy guidance, and treatment planning has amplified the demand for faster imaging protocols while maintaining high diagnostic quality. Conventional MRI acceleration strategies, including parallel imaging and compressed sensing, improve acquisition efficiency but remain limited by trade-offs involving signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), image sharpness, artifacts, and reconstruction complexity. Deep learning reconstruction (DLR) has emerged as a promising artificial intelligence-based approach for MRI acceleration and image enhancement. Unlike traditional reconstruction methods that rely primarily on predefined mathematical models, DLR uses neural networks to learn image priors and reconstruction features from MRI data. Published studies suggest that DLR may enable accelerated acquisitions while maintaining or, in some settings, improving image quality through denoising, artifact reduction, and improved spatial resolution and lesion conspicuity. However, these effects vary according to the reconstruction algorithm, sequence, acceleration factor, and clinical setting. Variational networks combine physics-based MRI constraints with learned regularization and represent an important framework for DLR. In prostate MRI, available studies have reported substantial reductions in acquisition time for T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted imaging while generally maintaining perceived image quality. Reported benefits include improved lesion conspicuity, reader confidence, and delineation of anatomic structures. Current evidence suggests that DLR generally preserves PI-RADS assessment and diagnostic performance rather than systematically altering lesion categorization; however, evidence demonstrating improvements in diagnostic accuracy or clinical outcomes remains limited. Important limitations include vendor and algorithm dependence, potential reconstruction artifacts, variability in quantitative imaging metrics, limited multicenter validation, and uncertain generalizability across scanners, protocols, and clinical settings. This review summarizes the technical principles underlying DLR, discusses current clinical applications in prostate MRI, highlights representative studies and workflow implications, reviews limitations, and outlines future directions for this rapidly evolving technology.

42913764.label: Purpose
42913764.text: We evaluated the preliminary efficacy of Empower lung cancer screening (LCS), a culturally adapted, multilevel intervention, compared with enhanced usual care (EUC) for improving LCS uptake among Hispanic patients.

42913764.label: Methods
42913764.text: In this pilot randomized controlled trial, Hispanic patients aged 50 to 80 years who met 2021 US Preventive Services Task Force LCS eligibility criteria were enrolled between February 2024 and August 2025. Participants were randomized 1:1 to EUC or Empower LCS. EUC included usual care plus a one-page educational handout. Empower LCS included a culturally adapted decision aid, provider notifications, patient text reminders, and health-related social needs support. The primary outcome was low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) ordering within 4 mo, assessed by medical record review or self-report. Analyses used chi-squared tests and logistic regressions.

42913764.label: Results
42913764.text: Sixty patients were randomized (mean age, 60.8 years ±7.4; 37 of 60 [61.7%] men; 21 of 60 [35.0%] Spanish-speaking). At 4 mo, LDCT ordering was higher with Empower LCS than with EUC (15 of 30 [50.0%] versus 4 of 30 [13.3%]; P = .002), as were LCS discussions (12 of 30 [40.0%] versus 5 of 30 [16.7%]; P = .045). LDCT completion was higher but not significant (9 of 30 [30.0%] versus 4 of 30 [13.3%]; P = .117), likely caused by small sample size. In exploratory adjusted models, Empower LCS was associated with higher odds of LDCT ordering (odds ratio, 7.32; 95% confidence interval, 1.97-34.16) and discussion (odds ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 1.20-16.28). Qualitative interviews identified provider trust and logistical barriers as drivers of screening engagement and completion, respectively.

42913764.label: Conclusions
42913764.text: Empower LCS increased LDCT ordering and screening discussions in this pilot trial. These findings support culturally tailored, low-cost, and scalable interventions to reduce disparities in LCS participation.

42957864.label: Objective
42957864.text: To evaluate the impact of a prostate imaging quality (PI-QUAL) v2 lecture on the accuracy and inter-reader agreement of prostate MRI image-quality assessment among radiologists and technologists from diverse professional backgrounds and institutions, and to evaluate its role in institutional-level quality improvement through a quality control (QC) process.

42957864.label: Materials and methods
42957864.text: Ten participants (five radiologists and five technologists) from five different hospitals independently evaluated 15 prostate MRIs before and after a standardized PI-QUAL v2 lecture. Reference scores were established by two experienced radiologists. Concordance with reference was assessed using accuracy and balanced accuracy. Inter-reader agreement was measured using percent agreement (PA) and Gwet's AC1. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on participant characteristics. For the quality assurance and QC (QA/QC), each center submitted 15 prostate MRIs before and after the lecture. Image quality was evaluated centrally to assess institutional improvement.

42957864.label: Results
42957864.text: Overall accuracy increased from 66.7% to 76.7%, and balanced accuracy increased from 62.9% to 84.2%; the mixed-effects model indicated significantly higher post-lecture accuracy (p = 0.038). Accuracy was also higher across all subgroups. Inter-reader agreement improved from PA 57.6% to 72.6% and Gwet's AC1 from 0.214 to 0.466. Through the QA/QC process, three centers initially failed to meet PI-QUAL v2 technical criteria. After feedback, all post-intervention scans achieved PI-QUAL v2 scores > 1.

42957864.label: Conclusion
42957864.text: A structured PI-QUAL v2 lecture improved both the accuracy and inter-reader agreement of prostate MRI image-quality assessments among diverse evaluators. Incorporating QA/QC further enhanced institutional image quality. PI-QUAL v2 training is a feasible strategy for standardizing prostate MRI quality.

42957864.label: Key points
42957864.text: Question Does a structured PI-QUAL v2 lecture for radiologists and technologists improve prostate MRI quality assessment performance and institutional imaging practice across institutions? Findings PI-QUAL v2 training improved accuracy (66.7% to 76.7%) and inter-reader agreement in prostate MRI quality assessment, while QA/QC feedback enhanced institutional imaging quality. Clinical relevance statement Structured PI-QUAL v2 education combined with quality assurance and quality control feedback improves evaluator consistency and institutional prostate MRI quality, facilitating standardized image-quality assessment and broader implementation of high-quality prostate MRI in clinical radiology.

42962514.label: Objectives
42962514.text: To develop and evaluate a multimodal fusion framework for the preoperative World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) low- and high-grade classification of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), integrating clinical characteristics, deep learning (DL), and radiomic signatures extracted from corticomedullary phase (CMP) contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) images.

42962514.label: Materials and methods
42962514.text: In this retrospective multicenter study, we evaluated a cohort of 1,052 patients with histologically verified ccRCC across four institutions. The data of the primary cohort (Center A, n = 665) were randomly divided into a training dataset (n = 465) and an internal validation dataset (n = 200). The data of 387 additional patients from three institutions (Centers B-D) constituted the independent external test set. Initial single-modality classifiers were developed via ensemble machine learning, utilizing clinical variables, multiscale radiomic data (capturing intratumoral, habitat, and peritumoral regions), and DL representations (2D, 2.5D, and 3D). A soft voting mechanism was subsequently applied to integrate the top-performing base models. Model interpretability was determined using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values, and overall diagnostic efficacy was quantified through receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

42962514.label: Results
42962514.text: The weighted soft voting model (SoftVote-Opt) showed the numerically highest AUC among the evaluated fusion strategies and single-modality models. This model yielded AUCs of 0.761 (95 % CI: 0.675-0.839) and 0.745 (95 % CI: 0.675-0.813), with corresponding MCCs of 0.347 (95 % CI: 0.217-0.475) and 0.302(95 % CI: 0.205 -0.387), within the internal validation and external test sets, respectively. SHAP analysis revealed peritumoral 5 mm radiomic features as the primary determinants of the model's output, followed by intratumoral radiomic features, whereas deep learning and clinical features offered lower relative contributions.

42962514.label: Conclusion
42962514.text: The multimodal fusion framework demonstrated moderate discriminatory performance across the internal validation and external test cohorts. These findings could be regarded as an exploratory study rather than evidence of established clinical superiority. The framework may provide complementary information for preoperative ccRCC grading.

42962514.label: Critical relevance statement
42962514.text: This study evaluates an exploratory multimodal fusion framework for preoperative ccRCC grading by combining clinical data, deep learning, and multiscale radiomic features. The framework may provide complementary non-invasive information for risk stratification.

42963514.text: Missed and misinterpreted injuries on the initial trauma CT remain a major source of delayed diagnosis and preventable morbidity. This pictorial essay illustrates, with cases from our department, the abdominal injuries most often overlooked: bowel and mesenteric injury, diaphragmatic rupture, hepatic and splenic vascular injury, renal vascular injury, pancreatic injury and bladder rupture. For each, we show the subtle direct and indirect CT signs, the mimickers that lead to over- or under-calling (including unidentified bright objects of the spleen), and the roles of multiphasic CT, multiplanar reformats, dual-energy CT, MRCP and CT cystography. We close with a practical search strategy and a low threshold for repeat imaging when the clinical course is discordant with the first scan.

42988564.text: [177Lu]Lu-PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) is increasingly administered worldwide in both inpatient and outpatient settings. Despite its growing use, there is no harmonized international guidance on what patients should be told before, during, and after therapy. This study aimed to capture current clinical practice and expert opinion to identify areas of consensus and divergence to develop a patient information template. Methods: An international survey was conducted among theranostic centers performing [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT. The questionnaire covered pretreatment procedures, therapy procedures, radiation precautions guidance, and posttreatment procedures. Inpatient and outpatient settings were evaluated separately. Results: In total, 102 centers from 23 countries participated. High agreement was observed for most pretreatment procedures, core therapy aspects, and general posttreatment guidance. In contrast, substantial variability was identified in posttreatment radiation precautions, particularly regarding distancing measures, duration of precautions, transportation after discharge, household and hygiene recommendations, and guidance affecting social interactions. Conclusion: This international survey demonstrated broad consensus for core clinical procedures but showed variability in posttreatment radiation precautions after RPT. By summarizing current practice and translating it into a patient information template, this project supports more consistent patient guidance across diverse clinical settings.

43020614.text: Repeatability of uptake in benign structures on prostate-specific membrane antigen PET is unexplored and poorly understood. We used a post hoc analysis of a test-retest cohort to assess repeatability of uptake in peripheral ganglia. Methods: Twenty-two patients were included. Spheric volumes of interest were manually placed on the cervical and lumbosacral dorsal root ganglia, the cervicothoracic ganglia, and the celiac ganglia. Repeatability was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficient, within-subject coefficient of variation, and Bland-Altman limits of agreement. Results: Ganglion uptake demonstrated an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.82 and a within-subject coefficient of variation of 13.1%. Bland-Altman analysis on a relative scale demonstrated that the mean bias was 0.9%, with 95% limits of agreement ranging from -35.8% to 37.6%, broadly comparable to the repeatability of prostate cancer tumors previously reported. Conclusion: The repeatability of uptake in peripheral ganglia on prostate-specific membrane antigen PET scans is similar to the repeatability of uptake in prostate cancer tumors. As such, isolated changes in uptake cannot be used as de facto evidence of a malignant lesion.
